Binary treatments and interaction effects

Source: vignettes/articles/binary-and-interactions.Rmd
binary-and-interactions.Rmd

A binary treatment

When the endogenous regressor is itself 0/1, its first stage is a probit and the average partial effect is a discrete change: the average difference in the probability of the outcome with the treatment switched on and off. apexog offers two estimators.

Control function with a probit first stage (firststage = "probit"; in Stata firststage(probit) or the i. prefix, (i.certified = subsidy)). The control function is the generalized residual of the first-stage probit. This is the estimator of Stata’s cfprobit with a probit first stage, and apexog reproduces it exactly, standard error included.

Recursive bivariate probit (firststage = "biprobit"). The outcome and the treatment are fitted jointly by maximum likelihood under bivariate normality of their errors, with the violation as an offset in the outcome equation. There is no generated regressor, so the standard errors are ordinary maximum-likelihood ones. The output also reports the estimated error correlation ρ.

The certification data were simulated with jointly normal errors (correlation 0.5), and the true average effect of certification on the probability of promotion is about 0.21:

data(certification)
cf <- apexog(promoted ~ tenure + manager, endog = certified ~ subsidy,
             data = certification, firststage = "probit",
             gmin = -0.10, gmax = 0.10, grid = 11, verbose = FALSE)
bp <- apexog(promoted ~ tenure + manager, endog = certified ~ subsidy,
             data = certification, firststage = "biprobit",
             gmin = -0.10, gmax = 0.10, grid = 11, verbose = FALSE)
rbind(control_function = cbind(cf$baseline[, c("estimate", "se")], confint(cf)),
      bivariate_probit = cbind(bp$baseline[, c("estimate", "se")], confint(bp)))
#>                   estimate         se      lower     upper
#> control_function 0.1996208 0.02949997 0.02038233 0.3813362
#> bivariate_probit 0.2163519 0.02650303 0.04807266 0.3846313
bp$rho
#>           
#> 0.4592555

Which one? The two rest on different assumptions, and neither set nests the other (Wooldridge 2014). The control function is consistent under Wooldridge’s sufficiency assumption, that the outcome error depends on the instrument and the treatment only through the generalized residual. It is only an approximation when the errors are jointly normal, the model the bivariate probit assumes. The approximation error grows with the correlation of the errors. In a large simulation (N = 400,000, true effect 0.211) the two-step estimate was:

Error correlation Control function Bias Bivariate probit Bias
0.3 0.205 −2.7% 0.211 0.0%
0.5 0.186 −11.6% 0.210 −0.4%
0.8 0.104 −50.6% 0.211 +0.1%

So when you maintain joint normality of the outcome and treatment errors, use the bivariate probit. apexog prints a note whenever a generalized-residual control function is in use. The same caveat applies to fractional ("fprobit") and count ("poisson") treatments, for which no exact alternative is available. The bivariate probit handles one endogenous regressor and the average partial effect, not interaction effects.

Interaction effects

In a probit the effect of one regressor depends on the values of all others, so the interaction of two variables is not read off a coefficient. apexog targets the average interaction effect (AIE) instead, averaged over the sample in the style of ginteff (Radean 2023). Three cases, detected from the data or set with aie_binary (in Stata with the c. and i. prefixes in target()):

Interactors AIE
continuous × continuous the average cross-partial derivative of the probability
continuous × binary the change in the continuous variable’s average slope when the binary one switches from 0 to 1
binary × binary the average second difference of the probability

Interactions of exogenous variables. aie = c("x", "w") with both among the controls. apexog adds the product x:w to the model (or uses it if the formula already contains it, as in x * w).

An endogenous treatment and a moderator. When the treatment is endogenous its product with a moderator is endogenous too, and needs its own instrument: the product of the instrument and the moderator. Declare the product as a second endogenous regressor and point aie at the pair. apexog then adds the product of the two control functions to the main probit (cfprobit’s cfinteract). In the promotion data training pays off more under a supportive manager:

data(promotion)
aie <- apexog(promoted ~ tenure + manager,
              endog = training + training:manager ~ subsidy + subsidy:manager,
              data = promotion, aie = c("training", "manager"),
              aie_binary = c(FALSE, TRUE),
              gmin = -0.05, gmax = 0.05, grid = 5, verbose = FALSE)
aie
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> Plausibly-exogenous AIE bounds (CHR 2012, UCI method)
#> Estimator: cfprobit  |  First stage: linear linear  |  SE: Murphy-Topel  |  N = 4000
#> Target:    Average Interaction Effect (training x manager): continuous-by-binary (first difference in manager)
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> Baseline (gamma = 0):
#>     AIE(training x manager) = 0.051042  (SE 0.012024)  [0.027475, 0.074609]
#> 
#> Scale:     1 latent-index unit of gamma = 0.2069 pr. points per unit of Z (avg., baseline)
#>            1 structural-latent unit of gamma = 1.2033 latent-index units  (sigma_tilde = 0.8310)
#> 
#> UCI union over gamma grid (5 point(s) per instrument):
#>     gamma_subsidy  range: [-0.0500, 0.0500]   exact Pr scale: [-0.0103, 0.0103]
#>     gamma_subsidy:manager range: [-0.0500, 0.0500]   exact Pr scale: [-0.0103, 0.0103]
#> 
#>     AIE(training x manager) bounds = [0.018002, 0.087606]
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The violation is now allowed on both instruments, the subsidy and its product with manager, each within ±0.05. With aie_binary = c(FALSE, TRUE) the AIE is the difference in training’s average slope between employees with and without a supportive manager: 0.051 at γ = 0, and between 0.018 and 0.088 over the range. The same model in Stata:

apexog uci promoted tenure manager ///
    (c.training c.training#c.manager = subsidy c.subsidy#i.manager), ///
    target(c.training#i.manager) gmin(-0.05) gmax(0.05) grid(5)
Baseline (gamma = 0):
    AIE(training ## manager) =  0.051042  (SE 0.012024)  [ 0.027475,  0.074609]
...
    AIE(training ## manager) bounds = [ 0.018002,  0.087606]

The control functions are held at their observed values when the moderator is switched, as in ginteff after the corresponding probit.

References

Radean, M. (2023). ginteff: A generalized command for computing interaction effects. Stata Journal, 23(2), 301–335. https://doi.org/10.1177/1536867X231175253

Wooldridge, J. M. (2014). Quasi-maximum likelihood estimation and testing for nonlinear models with endogenous explanatory variables. Journal of Econometrics, 182(1), 226–234. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2014.04.020
